raw_findings.message: Alice and Bob share a fixed source-controlled password, allowing anyone who knows the documented seeded credentials to authenticate to deployed instances.
Direct string equality can reveal how much of a presented token matches a stored token through response-time differences, enabling token-guessing attacks.
The limiter never records a new `windowStarted`, so it remains zero and every attempt resets the count, allowing unlimited password guesses from one address.
A login attempt with an unknown username makes `account` nil and panics when this line reads its password hash, producing a server error instead of rejecting the credentials.
Session tokens are derived from the current nanosecond timestamp, making them guessable from login timing and unsuitable as bearer credentials.
A successful login accepts an arbitrary external `next` URL and redirects the browser to it, enabling trusted-site open-redirect phishing.
Any authenticated user can choose another account's `user` query value and retrieve that profile because the handler never checks that the requested account belongs to the bearer user.
The profile response exposes unsalted SHA-1 password hashes, including the admin hash, allowing attackers to perform offline password cracking.
An authenticated caller controls the URL passed to `http.Get`, allowing requests to loopback, private-network, or other reachable internal services.
The default HTTP client has no timeout, so a caller can make proxy requests to nonresponsive upstreams that hold server handlers and connections indefinitely.
Rotation only changes `signingKey`, which is not used to sign or validate sessions, so previously issued bearer tokens remain valid after rotation.
The unauthenticated health endpoint returns the active signing key, exposing secret configuration to any caller.
Every deployment uses the source-controlled admin password, so anyone who knows or obtains the code can log in as an administrator.

The admin account is created only when `ADMIN_PASSWORD` is set, so the documented seeded admin account and `/rotate` functionality are unavailable in a default launch.
The login decoder accepts an unbounded body, allowing a client to submit an enormous password value that consumes excessive memory and hashing time.
Every successful login adds a session that is never expired or evicted, allowing repeated logins to grow the map indefinitely and make session lookups increasingly costly.
When `next` is supplied, the handler redirects without returning the newly created bearer token or setting a cookie, so the client cannot authenticate subsequent requests with that session.

raw_findings.message: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, allowing a database or source-code reader to crack them efficiently with offline guessing.
Direct string equality can take longer when more token bytes match, allowing repeated comparisons to reveal valid token contents through timing.
The rate-limit window is never updated from its zero value, so every login attempt resets the counter and clients can make unlimited guesses.
A login using an unknown username makes account nil and panics when its PasswordHash is read, returning a server error and flooding server logs if repeated.
Session tokens are generated from the current timestamp rather than cryptographic randomness, so an attacker who can estimate a login time can guess valid tokens.
The login handler redirects to an unvalidated next value, so a crafted login URL can send users to an attacker-controlled site.
The handler uses the caller-supplied user query without checking it against the authenticated user, so any valid account can retrieve another account's profile.
The profile response exposes each account's password hash to any authenticated user, enabling offline password cracking.
An authenticated user can choose an arbitrary URL for http.Get, allowing requests to loopback, private-network, or other reachable services.
Rotating the signing key does not affect the sessions map used for authentication, so previously issued tokens remain valid after rotation.
The unauthenticated health endpoint returns the signing key, exposing signing configuration to any client that can reach the server.
The administrator password is compiled into the source, so anyone who can inspect the binary or repository can obtain credentials that grant administrator access.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Alice and Bob are created with the fixed, source-visible password `bluebird42`, so anyone who can reach the loopback service can authenticate as either seeded user.
Without `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, no admin account is created, so the documented admin account and `/rotate` functionality are unavailable on a default start.
The login decoder has no body-size limit, so a local client can submit an enormous JSON password and force the server to allocate excessive memory while decoding it.
A successful login stores a session before validating or handling `next`, and requests using `next` never receive the token, allowing repeated logins to accumulate unusable sessions indefinitely.

When a valid `next` value is supplied, the handler redirects without returning the newly created token or setting it in a cookie, so the client cannot authenticate subsequent requests with that login.

raw_findings.message: Passwords are verified with unsalted SHA-1, which is too fast for password storage and makes stolen hashes inexpensive to crack.
Token equality uses an early-exit string comparison, so response timing can reveal how much of a guessed token matches.
Session authentication only checks the in-memory token map and never uses the signing key or epoch, so rotating the key leaves existing bearer tokens valid.
The limiter never updates `windowStarted`, so it remains zero and every attempt resets the count, allowing unlimited login guesses.
An unknown username makes `account` nil, and dereferencing it panics the login handler instead of returning an invalid-credentials response.
Session tokens are derived directly from the current nanosecond timestamp, making bearer credentials guessable from their issuance time.
A successful login redirects to the unrestricted `next` value, so an attacker can send users through the gateway to a phishing site.
The handler uses the caller-controlled `user` query parameter without checking that the authenticated user may view that account, allowing any logged-in user to read other profiles.
Every authenticated user can retrieve each account's password hash, enabling offline password cracking, especially because the hashes use unsalted SHA-1.
Any authenticated user can make the gateway fetch an arbitrary target, including loopback or internal services, by supplying it in the `target` query parameter.
The unauthenticated health endpoint returns the active signing key, exposing secret configuration to any caller.
The administrator password is embedded in source, allowing anyone with the code to log in as an administrator using the fixed password.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Sessions have no expiration and remain valid in the map until rotation or process restart, so a stolen bearer token can be reused indefinitely.
Alice and Bob always receive the source-defined password `bluebird42`, so anyone who can reach the gateway can authenticate as either seeded user without an administrator configuring credentials.
Without `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, the default startup omits the admin account, despite the README listing it as seeded, so the documented default setup cannot authenticate an administrator or use `/rotate`.
The login handler decodes the request body without a size limit, so a client can submit a huge JSON body and force unbounded memory allocation.

The handler stores a new session before processing `next`, but a successful redirect returns neither the token nor a session cookie, leaving the redirected client unable to authenticate and the stored session inaccessible.
